details:
**Gitanjali (Song Offerings)** – The poetry collection that earned Tagore the 1913 Nobel Prize; its title translates as “Song Offerings” and is the work most frequently cited in quizbowl questions.

**Opening line “Thou hast made me endless, such is thy pleasure.”** – The famous first line of Gitanjali, often quoted to signal Tagore’s authorship; it appears in many clues as the introductory verse of the collection.

**“Where the mind is without fear”** – A well‑known poem from Gitanjali (also appearing in the larger “Jana Gana Mana” context) that describes an ideal, free society; it is repeatedly used as a hallmark of Tagore’s vision.

**“Father, let my country awake.”** – The concluding line of the same poem that contains “Where the mind is without fear,” frequently cited as a rallying call and a signature Tagore phrase.

**Jana Gana Mana (Indian national anthem)** – The lyrics of India’s national anthem were penned by Tagore; questions often pair this fact with his authorship of Gitanjali.

**W. B. Yeats’s preface/foreword** – The Irish poet wrote the introduction to the English edition of Gitanjali, a detail that uniquely links Tagore to Western literary circles and appears in many clues.

**The Post Office (play)** – Tagore’s short drama in which a sick child named Amal writes to the king; it was famously read by André Gide on the eve of Paris’s fall and is a recurrent clue.

**“Victory, victory, victory to thee”** – A refrain from a poem praising a “ruler of the minds of all people,” often quoted to identify Tagore’s patriotic verse.

**“Song Offerings” translation** – The English title given to Gitanjali when it was published abroad; recognizing this translation helps pinpoint Tagore among other Indian writers.

**First Asian (non‑Western) Nobel laureate in Literature (1913)** – Tagore’s historic Nobel win is a standout biographical clue that distinguishes him from other poets.

**“The Golden Boat” (collection)** – Another of Tagore’s poetry compilations; the title and its theme of a “golden boat” appear in several questions.

**Bard of Bengal (or Biswakabi/Bishwokobi)** – A common epithet for Tagore used in quizbowl prompts; recognizing this nickname directly points to him.

**Andre Gide’s 1940 radio reading** – The French writer’s broadcast of Tagore’s play (The Post Office) on the night Paris fell; this historical anecdote uniquely identifies Tagore’s work.
